title: Modbus RTU framing and CRC, byte by byte
summary: One real request frame taken apart byte by byte - address, function, data, and the CRC-16 that guards it - plus the response it earns.

blocks.title: Eight bytes that ask a question
blocks.body: Modbus RTU has run factory floors since 1979 because it is small enough to hold in your head. A master sends a frame, a slave answers. This page takes one real request apart byte by byte, including the two CRC bytes that let the receiver prove the message arrived intact.

items.label: The classic line setting - baud, data bits, even parity, one stop bit
Usable slave addresses on one bus; 0 broadcasts to all
The silence that frames a message - about 4 ms at 9600 baud

nodes.title: Address - 1 byte
nodes.detail: Which slave is being spoken to. Everyone else stays quiet.

nodes.title: Function - 1 byte
nodes.detail: What to do: read coils, read registers, write, and so on.

nodes.title: Data - 0 to 252 bytes
nodes.detail: The arguments: starting address and quantity for a read, values for a write.

nodes.title: CRC - 2 bytes
nodes.detail: CRC-16 over everything before it, low byte sent first.

blocks.heading: The address byte
blocks.body: Every slave on the bus listens to every frame, but only the addressed one answers. Address 0 is the broadcast address: all slaves act on it and none reply, which makes it useful for writes that must land everywhere at once and useless for anything that needs confirmation. Valid slave addresses are 1 through 247; 248 to 255 are reserved.

blocks.heading: The function codes you actually meet
rows: Reads read-only 16-bit registers, often sensor values
Writes a block of holding registers at once
blocks.caption: Coils and discrete inputs are bits; holding and input registers are 16-bit words.

blocks.heading: One real request, byte by byte
rows: Starting address, low byte - start at register 0
blocks.caption: 01 03 00 00 00 02 C4 0B: device 1, give me holding registers 0 and 1.

blocks.heading: The answer that comes back
rows: Function - echo of the request's function
Byte count - 4 data bytes follow (2 registers)
blocks.caption: 01 03 04 00 2A 01 8F 9B CF: two registers, values 42 and 399.

blocks.title: Two byte orders, both on purpose
blocks.body: Register data inside the frame is big-endian: high byte first, so 00 2A reads naturally as 42. The CRC is the exception - it is sent low byte first, so the value 0x0BC4 appears on the wire as C4 then 0B. Mixing these up is the classic first-week bug in a Modbus implementation.

blocks.heading: What the CRC is for
blocks.body: The line is electrically hostile: long runs, motor noise, loose terminals. Parity catches some single-bit flips but nothing fancier. The CRC-16 is a 16-bit remainder computed over the whole frame - address, function, and data - so any burst of noise that changes the message almost certainly changes the remainder. The receiver recomputes it and compares; a mismatch means the frame is discarded, not acted on.

blocks.heading: Computing the CRC-16, the algorithm
items: Start with a 16-bit register set to all ones: 0xFFFF.
XOR the first byte of the frame into the low byte of the register.
Shift the register right one bit. If the bit that fell off the end was a 1, XOR the register with 0xA001.
Repeat the shift step eight times - once per bit of the byte.
XOR in the next byte and repeat, for every byte of address, function, and data - but not the CRC itself.
The final register is the CRC. Send the low byte first, then the high byte.

blocks.heading: The same algorithm as pseudocode
Why 0xA001
blocks.body: That constant is the Modbus polynomial - x^16 + x^15 + x^2 + 1 - written in the reversed bit order the right-shifting algorithm needs. It is the same polynomial as CRC-16-IBM. You do not need to derive it to use it, but recognizing 0xA001 in someone's code is how you know you are looking at a Modbus CRC and not one of the many other 16-bit CRCs.

blocks.heading: Silence is the frame marker
blocks.body: RTU frames have no start flag or length header. A message begins after at least 3.5 character-times of silence on the bus and ends the same way, and the bytes inside must arrive with gaps under 1.5 character-times or the receiver treats the frame as broken. At 9600 baud, one character takes about 1.1 ms, so the framing silence is about 4 ms. This is why a Modbus master must pace its transmissions and why jittery software timers can corrupt a bus.

blocks.title: When the slave says no
blocks.body: An exception response sets the function code's top bit - a reply to function 03 comes back as 83 - followed by one exception byte: 01 illegal function, 02 illegal data address, 03 illegal data value, 04 slave device failure. A request for register 9000 on a device with ten registers earns 01 83 02 plus its CRC.

blocks.heading: Check the frame
blocks.prompt: In the request 01 03 00 00 00 02 C4 0B, which byte carries the function code?
blocks.explanation: Address comes first, function second. Byte 1 is the slave address 01, byte 2 is function 03 (Read Holding Registers), and the last two bytes are the CRC.

blocks.heading: Check the guard
blocks.prompt: Which bytes does the CRC-16 cover?
options: Address, function, and data - everything before the CRC
The whole frame including the CRC bytes themselves
blocks.explanation: The CRC is computed over the entire message up to the CRC field. That is what lets the receiver recompute it over what it received and compare against the two bytes that followed.
